projects.title: Croft End
projects.description: A light-filled city apartment transformed into a calm and considered sanctuary.

body.text: Working with Constraints

At 780 square feet, Croft End required careful thinking about what the space needed to do versus what it needed to feel like. The client — a single professional who works from home three days a week — needed the apartment to function as an office, a living room, and a place to decompress, all without those functions bleeding into one another.

We reconfigured the layout entirely, removing a partition wall to merge the kitchen and living area, and using a bespoke joinery unit to define the workspace without closing it off. The unit houses a fold-down desk, concealed shelving, and a slim wardrobe on its reverse face — allowing the client to close the day behind literal doors at the end of the afternoon.
Light and Storage

The apartment faces north, so maximizing the sense of light was a central concern throughout. We kept the palette extremely pale — white walls, ash flooring, and linen curtains that pool gently on the floor — and introduced a large mirror opposite the main window to push daylight further into the plan.

Storage was treated as an architectural element rather than an afterthought. Floor-to-ceiling cabinetry lines the hallway, providing generous capacity without interrupting the main living areas. The result is a home that feels twice its size — uncluttered, quiet, and entirely at ease.

projects.title: Vale House
projects.description: Full home renovation for a family in the suburbs, focused on natural materials.

body.text: The Brief

The clients approached us with a clear vision: breathe new life into their 1990s suburban home without losing its warmth. Every room needed to work harder for a growing family while feeling considered and unhurried. We stripped the interior back to its shell and rebuilt the layout around how the family actually lives — morning routines, homework, weekend cooking.

The ground floor was opened up to create a continuous living and dining area, anchored by a central kitchen island crafted from honed limestone. Light became the guiding principle, with new skylights introduced above the stairwell to draw afternoon sun deep into the plan.
Materials and Finish

We leaned into a palette of natural, tactile materials that would age gracefully — white oak flooring, linen upholstery, and hand-plastered walls in a warm off-white. Fixtures were kept simple and matte throughout, letting the textures carry the room rather than decorative detail.

Custom cabinetry runs the length of the utility hall, concealing the practical demands of family life behind clean, flush doors. Every finish was sampled on-site across different times of day before being signed off, ensuring the palette holds under both the bright Texas sun and the warm glow of evening light.

projects.title: Westport
projects.description: A beachside cottage redesigned as a year-round family home, blending casual coastal living with refined detail.

body.text: The Brief

Westport started as a seasonal getaway — a compact beach cottage used for a few months a year, furnished with whatever was comfortable and expendable. The clients, a family of four, decided to make it their permanent home and asked us to transform it accordingly without disturbing the easygoing character that made them love it in the first place.

The challenge was to make the home feel complete and considered without losing its sense of ease. We restructured the interior to prioritize the view — pulling the living area toward the ocean-facing elevation and reducing the footprint of secondary rooms to give the main spaces room to breathe.
Palette and Texture

The material palette was drawn entirely from the immediate landscape: bleached linen, whitewashed timber, and matte ceramic in shades of sand and fog. We deliberately avoided anything that read as nautical or themed, opting instead for a quiet warmth that works in every season and in every light.

Outdoor and indoor materials were kept consistent across the threshold — the same stone used on the terrace continues into the kitchen — creating a sense of the house extending naturally into the garden. The result feels less like a renovated cottage and more like a home that was always meant to be exactly this.

projects.title: Birch Lane
projects.description: A newly built family home where every interior space was designed from the ground up.

body.text: Collaborating from the Ground Up

Birch Lane gave us the rare opportunity to work alongside the architects from the very beginning of the build, before a single wall was framed. This kind of early collaboration meant we could influence decisions that are usually fixed by the time an interior designer arrives — structural openings, ceiling heights, window placement, and the routing of services.

The family had a strong sense of what they wanted: a home that connected to the surrounding Douglas fir forest while remaining practical for two young children. We responded with a palette rooted in the landscape — pale stone, unfinished timber, and a muted range of greens pulled directly from the treeline outside.
Joinery and Detail

All joinery was designed in-house and fabricated by a local Portland workshop. The kitchen runs along an entire wall of the open-plan ground floor, finished in a painted sage with unlacquered brass hardware that will patinate over time. A built-in window seat in the reading nook doubles as storage, with cushions upholstered in a durable wool check.

Upstairs, each bedroom was treated as a distinct space rather than a repeated formula. The children's rooms feature built-in beds with integrated shelving, while the primary suite opens through glazed doors onto a private terrace framed by birch trees — the detail that gave the project its name.

projects.title: Meridian
projects.description: A boutique co-working space designed to feel warm and residential, not corporate.

body.text: Concept

Meridian was commissioned by a hospitality group looking to create a members-only workspace that felt like a well-designed home rather than an office. The brief called for a space that could support focused solo work in the morning and informal client meetings by the afternoon — all within a single, coherent interior.

We organized the floor plan into a series of distinct zones — a library-style quiet room, a communal table beneath a grid of pendant lights, and a series of semi-enclosed booths upholstered in deep green velvet. The reception was treated as a living room, with a curved sofa and a fireplace to anchor arrivals.
Furniture and Lighting

All furniture was sourced from independent American makers, with a focus on solid wood frames and natural upholstery. We avoided anything that read as office equipment — task chairs were replaced with dining-weight seating, and every desk surface was topped with leather rather than laminate.

Lighting was layered across three circuits to allow the mood of the space to shift throughout the day. Wall sconces provide a steady ambient base, while adjustable pendants over the work surfaces give members control over their immediate environment. The result is a space that members consistently describe as somewhere they actually want to spend time.

projects.title: Studio Six
projects.description: A photography studio and showroom designed to double as a flexible event venue for a creative agency.

body.text: A Space That Works Twice

Studio Six occupies the ground floor of a converted warehouse in the Arts District, taken on by a creative agency that needed a professional shoot environment by day and a client-facing event space by evening. The brief was precise: every design decision had to serve both uses without compromise, and the transformation between modes had to be achievable by a two-person team in under an hour.

We resolved this with a track system running the full length of the ceiling, allowing large fabric panels to divide or open the space in minutes. The shooting area is anchored by a seamless white cyclorama on one end and a practical kitchen counter on the other — both of which read as intentional design elements rather than functional afterthoughts when the space is configured for events.
Finishes and Flexibility

Every surface was chosen for how it photographs as much as how it lives. The floors are a warm poured concrete, the walls a true white that holds color accurately under both tungsten and daylight-balanced lighting. A long custom credenza along the east wall provides equipment storage that doubles as a buffet surface during evening events.

The existing warehouse windows were retained and fitted with motorized blackout blinds, giving the team full control over natural light without sacrificing the raw character of the original building. It is a space built around performance — and it delivers on both its roles without ever feeling like it is compromising on either.

projects.title: The Granary
projects.description: A converted warehouse reimagined as a creative studio and event space for a design firm.

body.text: Transforming the Shell

The Granary began as a raw 1940s warehouse in Nashville's Wedgewood-Houston arts district — concrete floors, exposed steel trusses, and a roof that had seen better decades. The client, a growing design and branding firm, needed a space that could serve as their permanent studio while also hosting client presentations, product launches, and community events.

Rather than softening the building's industrial character, we leaned into it. The original trusses were sandblasted and left exposed, the concrete floor was ground and sealed to a polished finish, and the brick perimeter walls were repointed and left bare. Against this honest backdrop, we introduced warm, considered elements — custom oak shelving, a long blackened steel kitchen counter, and a lighting scheme that shifts the room from working daylight to warm evening ambiance.
Balancing Work and Gathering

The floor plan was organized around a central spine that separates the open-plan studio from the event and presentation zone. A full-height sliding partition — crafted from reclaimed Douglas fir — allows the two areas to be merged for large gatherings or fully separated for focused studio work. The system required no track in the ceiling, preserving the drama of the exposed trusses above.

Acoustic panels were integrated discreetly into the wall system, ensuring the space remains functional at volume without sacrificing its visual rawness. The result is a workplace that the firm's team describes as the first space they've ever truly not wanted to leave at the end of the day.

projects.title: Elmwood
projects.description: A custom new build for a couple transitioning from city to suburban life, designed to feel rooted and enduring.

body.text: Designing for the Long Term

Elmwood was a project built on a single conviction: that a well-designed home should feel better with age, not in spite of it. The clients — a couple in their early forties moving out of a city apartment for the first time — wanted a house that would grow with them, accommodate guests comfortably, and never require the kind of wholesale update that fashion-driven interiors eventually demand.

We focused the design around a handful of architectural gestures that would remain timeless: a double-height entrance hall, a generous kitchen running the depth of the house, and a covered back porch that extends the living space into the Colorado outdoors for most of the year. Everything else followed from those anchors.
Materials Built to Last

The material selection was governed by one question: how will this look in twenty years? Brick was chosen for the exterior and carried inside as a feature wall in the living room. Flooring is solid white oak throughout — not engineered — chosen for its ability to be sanded and refinished across decades of use. Hardware is unlacquered bronze, expected and welcomed to patinate.

The kitchen was designed with the same philosophy: shaker-profile cabinetry in a deep charcoal, stone countertops with a honed rather than polished finish, and open shelving in lieu of upper cabinets to keep the room feeling connected rather than closed. Elmwood is a home that already feels lived-in, in the best possible way.

projects.title: The Mill
projects.description: A 19th-century textile mill converted into a boutique hotel lobby and shared guest areas.

body.text: Honoring the Original

The Mill is one of those rare commissions where the building itself was the brief. A mid-19th-century textile mill in Providence's Olneyville neighborhood, it had passed through several owners and uses before being acquired by a hospitality group with a specific vision: a small, serious hotel for design-minded travelers who wanted character over comfort-by-formula.

Our role was to design the lobby, bar, library, and breakfast room — the guest-facing common areas that would set the tone for the whole property. We began by doing as little as possible, stripping back decades of accumulated renovation to reveal the mill's original structural bones: heavy timber posts, cast iron columns, wide plank floors, and brick walls that still bore the faint marks of the looms that once stood against them.
Layering New onto Old

Against the exposed historic fabric, we introduced a curated layer of contemporary furniture and lighting — pieces with enough visual weight to hold their own in the high-ceilinged spaces without competing with the architecture. The bar counter is solid marble, the library shelving is blackened steel, and the lounge seating is upholstered in a deep ochre mohair that reads warmly against the red brick.

Custom pendant lights — a collaboration with a Providence glassblower — hang in clusters over the main lobby, casting a warm, shifting light that changes with the time of day. The result is a space that guests describe as feeling both very old and very present — which was precisely the ambition from the first conversation with the client.

articles.title: Why We Draw the Daylight Before the Plan.
articles.description: We set the daylight study before the first plan, because a room’s hours decide its purpose.
articles.author: Mara Idrissi

body.text: We start with the sun.

Every project in the studio opens with a daylight study, drawn before any plan. We log the path of the sun across the site for four dates in the year, then mark the hours each room can expect. The study takes a week, and it settles questions that would otherwise be argued for months.

The method came out of a 2019 apartment in Lisbon where the client wanted the kitchen on the street side. The study showed that face held direct light for under two hours in winter. We moved the kitchen to the courtyard and kept the street side for the study, which needed even light rather than warmth.
Rooms follow their hours.

Once the hours are mapped, program follows. A room that holds morning light becomes a kitchen or a place to read. A room that holds late light becomes a place to sit after work. Rooms with thin light become storage, circulation, or bathrooms, where glare would be a nuisance anyway.

This reverses the usual order, in which the plan is fixed and the lighting is corrected afterward with fixtures. Correcting with fixtures is expensive, and it never quite works. A south window is not a lamp.
What the study cannot answer.

The study says nothing about view, noise, or the neighbors, and we weigh all three separately. On a 2024 house in Porto the best-lit face looked onto a service road, so we accepted a dimmer room and borrowed light through a clerestory.
The point is not that daylight wins every argument. The point is that it enters the argument first, while the plan is still cheap to change.

articles.title: The Case for Lime Plaster in Coastal Houses.
articles.description: Lime plaster costs more to apply and less to keep, and it changes how a wall meets the light.
articles.author: Joost Haverkamp

body.text: Why we specify it.

Lime plaster has been in our standard specification since 2021. It is applied in three coats over four days, which is longer than gypsum board and skim, and it costs roughly forty percent more on the first pass. The case for it is what happens over the following decade.
Lime takes up and releases moisture rather than trapping it. In the stone houses we work on along the coast, that single property removes most of the damp problems that synthetic finishes create.
How it reads in a room.

A lime wall is slightly uneven, and the unevenness is the point. Light grazes across it and reveals the trowel, so a flat wall carries a faint texture through the day instead of sitting dead. Photographs flatten this almost entirely, which is why we ask clients to visit a finished wall before deciding.

The color sits inside the material, mixed with pigment rather than painted on top. A scuff exposes more of the same color instead of a white substrate, so the wall ages without needing a touch-up kit.
Where it is the wrong choice.
Lime is alkaline and slow to cure, and it does not belong behind a shower or on a surface that will be washed daily. We use tile or stone there and keep lime to the dry rooms.
It also needs a plasterer who has done it before. On a 2022 project we lost two weeks to a crew learning on site, and the finish still had to be floated again.

articles.title: How We Scope a Project in Four Weeks.
articles.description: A fixed four-week opening stage, priced separately, so both sides can leave before the expensive part begins.
articles.author: Noor Benali

body.text: The opening stage.

Every engagement starts with the same four weeks, priced on its own and not folded into the project fee. It covers a survey, the daylight study, a program written with the client, and three plan options at 1:100.

At the end of the four weeks either side can stop, and the client keeps the drawings. We have ended five engagements this way since 2020, and in each case the reason surfaced in week two rather than month eight.
What we ask for.
We need a budget figure, a date that matters, and the name of the person who decides. Projects without all three tend to produce drawings that please everyone in the room and no one afterward.

We also ask for photographs of rooms the client likes, including rooms they cannot explain. Those are more useful than a list of styles, because they tend to share a quality of light rather than a look.
After the four weeks.
The full fee is set once the program is fixed, as a percentage of construction cost with a floor. We publish the floor, which in 2026 is 18,000 euros, so a small project is not quoted into silence.
From there the stages are conventional: design development, construction drawings, tender, and site. The difference is that the brief arriving at design development has already been tested.

articles.title: The Harbor House, Reduced to Its Frame.
articles.description: A 1930s warehouse on the Setúbal waterfront, reduced to its frame and rebuilt as one long room.
articles.author: Mara Idrissi

body.text: What we found.

The building was put up in 1934 as a salt store, and it had been divided into eleven rooms by the time we saw it in 2023. Behind the partitions was a concrete frame in good condition, nine bays long, with a clear height of four and a half meters.
Almost all of our work was removal. We took out every internal wall, two added floors, and a rear extension, which gave back a single volume of 240 square meters with light from both long faces.
One room, four thresholds.

Rather than rebuild rooms, we placed four freestanding volumes along the north wall: a kitchen core, a bathroom, a pair of bedrooms, and a stair to the roof. None of them touches the ceiling, so the original frame reads continuously overhead.

The gaps between the volumes do the work that corridors usually do. Each one is wide enough to stand in and to hold a door, a bench, or a bookcase, and they give the long room a rhythm at roughly six-meter intervals.
Materials and cost.
The frame was left as found, washed and sealed. New work is lime plaster, oak, and blackened steel, held to three materials so the volumes read as objects set inside an older building.

The project was delivered in fourteen months at 1,850 euros per square meter, which was under the budget set in 2023. The saving came almost entirely from demolition, since the frame needed no structural repair.
Living in it.

The owners moved in during the spring of 2025 and have since reported one problem and one surprise. The problem is acoustic: a single long room carries sound, and they added a rug and two curtains in the first month.
The surprise is the roof. We treated the stair as circulation, and it has turned into the room the family uses most between May and September.

articles.title: Two Weeks of Pencil Before the First File.
articles.description: The first fifty drawings of any project are made in pencil, at a desk, before a file is opened.
articles.author: Noor Benali

body.text: Pencil first, for two weeks.

Each project begins with a sketchbook and a fixed rule: no computer drawings for the first two weeks. By the end of that period we usually have between forty and sixty plans and sections, most of them wrong, all of them quick.

The rule exists because the model rewards resolution too early. A drawn wall in a modeling program has a thickness, a material, and a cost, and once it has those it is hard to throw away. A pencil wall is a line.
Scale on the page.

We draw plans at 1:100 and details at 1:5, by hand, on tracing paper laid over the last version. Working in layers means the history of the idea stays visible, so an option abandoned on Tuesday can be recovered on Friday without redrawing it.
Dimensions go on the drawing from the first sheet. A sketch without numbers is a mood, and a mood cannot be checked against a stair riser or a door swing.
When the file opens.

The model begins once the plan has stopped moving, and from that point it is a record rather than a tool for thinking. Construction drawings, schedules, and coordination all live there, and they stay accurate because the arguments were settled on paper.
Clients receive both. The drawings explain the intent, and the model explains the building.

articles.title: Four Oak Floors, Thirty Years Later.
articles.description: We revisited four floors we laid between 1996 and 2004 to see what the oil, the traffic, and the light had done.
articles.author: Joost Haverkamp

body.text: Four floors, four conditions.

In 2025 we went back to four oak floors the studio specified between 1996 and 2004: two apartments, a bookshop, and a family house. All four were twenty-millimeter solid boards, oiled rather than lacquered, and all four are still in service.
The variable we had not accounted for was traffic. The bookshop floor has worn through to bare wood along one three-meter line, and the apartments show almost no wear outside the kitchens.
What the oil did.

Oiled oak darkens, and it darkens unevenly. Boards under a south window in the family house are two shades lighter than boards under the sofa, which the owners had expected to be the other way around. Direct sun bleaches faster than it ambers.
Maintenance has been modest. Three of the four have been re-oiled once, at between eleven and eighteen years, and the bookshop has been done four times.
What we changed.

We now specify a twenty-two-millimeter board rather than twenty, which buys one more sanding over the life of the floor. In commercial work we lay the boards across the main line of travel so wear spreads over more joints.
We have kept the oil. A lacquered floor fails all at once and has to be stripped, while an oiled floor fails slowly and in one place, which an owner can live with and repair.
